history.notes: The drill progression is anonymous modern instructional practice. preconditions: A player working without sight of the board
false_positive_traps: This describes a player's skill, not a position. It cannot be attached to a move.

typical_plans: Name square colours until it is automatic
Trace knight routes between squares mentally
Play simple endgames unseen before whole games
strategic_consequences: Fluency in the board frees attention for the position

exceptions: Blindfold play is an advanced application, not a starting point; the drills come first.
Fine reported that a blank board was a hindrance rather than a help to him, while other players found it useful - individual variation is real.
limitations: No controlled evidence is known to this base that these drills improve playing strength.
The historical claims recorded here (al-Adli, the Najdorf and Koltanowski records) come from a low-confidence source and are unverified.

by_level.beginner: Knowing the board itself without looking - which squares are light or dark, and where a knight can go.
by_level.intermediate: Board vision. Practise square colours and knight routes until they are automatic, then try simple endings unseen.
by_level.advanced: Fluency in the relations is the substrate the blindfold representation is built on; computing them costs attention the position needs.
by_level.master: Worth noting that the transfer of these drills to playing strength is asserted rather than demonstrated.

by_depth.short: Knowing the board without looking at it.
by_depth.normal: Board vision: fluent knowledge of the board itself - square colours, piece routes, which squares connect to which - held without needing to see it. It is the layer beneath blindfold play, and the standard drills build it before any whole game is attempted.
by_depth.deep: The foundation beneath holding a position unseen: before the position can be held without the board, the board must be. The drill progression is consistent across sources - square colours, then piece routes, then following a knight, then reconstructing small positions, then simple endgames unseen - with the knight's tour the most-recommended single exercise. Why it plausibly matters follows from the research on representation: if what a player holds is relational rather than pictorial, fluency in those relations is exactly the substrate, and effort spent computing them is effort not spent on the position. What is not established is that any of it raises playing strength.

explanations.hedge: The drills are widely recommended, but this base knows of no controlled evidence that they transfer to playing strength.
explanations.lesson: Learn the board before trying to hold a position on it.

beginner_words: seeing where the knight can go

definition_short: Fluent knowledge of the board itself — where each square is, what colour it is, and how pieces travel between squares — held without needing to look.
definition_long:
The foundation layer beneath blindfold play. Before a player can hold a POSITION without sight of the board, they need the BOARD without sight of it: which squares are light and which dark, which squares a knight on a given square reaches, which diagonal connects two squares.

THE STANDARD DRILL PROGRESSION is consistent across instructional sources: name the colour of a named square; trace a piece's route between two squares; follow a knight's path without a board; reconstruct a small position from brief exposure; then play out simple endgames unseen before attempting whole games. The KNIGHT'S TOUR — visiting all sixty-four squares in sixty-three legal knight moves — is the most-recommended single exercise, and it is very old; Murray traced tours to al-Adli ar-Rumi around 840 AD.

WHY IT PLAUSIBLY MATTERS is consistent with the research on representation. If what a blindfold player holds is relational rather than pictorial, then fluency in the relations — this square is dark, that knight reaches these squares — is exactly the substrate the representation is built on, and effort spent computing it is effort not spent on the position.

WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED is that these drills improve playing strength. That claim is made confidently by instructional sources and this base has found no controlled study supporting it. The honest statement is that the drills train the specific skills they exercise, and that those skills are prerequisites for blindfold play.
